title: A 99%-accurate alarm can be wrong 99 times out of 100 when it goes off
body: Imagine a city of a million, 100 of them terrorists, and a camera that spots 99% of terrorists and wrongly flags 1% of everyone else. About 99 of the 100 terrorists trigger the alarm, but so do about 9,999 of the 999,900 innocent people, so someone who sets it off is a terrorist in only about 99 of 10,098 cases, under 1%. Expecting 99% instead is the **base rate fallacy**: ignoring how rare the thing you are hunting is. Bayes’ theorem gives the right answer, though it isn’t how most people think; in court the same slip is the prosecutor’s fallacy.

slides.alt: Animation styled as a lab report: a city of 1,000,000 drawn as dots of 100 people, one dot holding all 100 terrorists, 99 of them flagged, and 9,999 innocent people flagged too. Keeping only the 10,098 flagged people shows just 99 are terrorists: 0.98%.

slides.heading: Who sets off the alarm, in a city of a million
slides.note: The camera spots 99% of the 100 terrorists and wrongly flags 1% of the other 999,900.

slides.question: 1 in 1,000 drivers is drunk; the breathalyser wrongly flags 5% of sober ones. Chance a flagged driver is drunk?
slides.explanation: Many people say 95%. It is about 2%: for every drunk driver caught, about 50 sober drivers also fail the test.

slides.heading: The breathalyser version
slides.text: Per 1,000 drivers there is one drunk driver, who fails the test, and about 50 sober drivers who also fail, 5% of 999. So of roughly 51 failed tests, just one belongs to a drunk driver: about 2%. The same arithmetic, written formally, is Bayes’ theorem.

slides.heading: In court
slides.text: The prosecutor’s fallacy is the same slip in a courtroom: assuming that the chance of a random match, such as a shared blood type, equals the chance that the defendant is innocent. It ignores how many other people in the population would match too.
